migrationNotes: Spine: follow the water. A cup of squash shows that strength depends on volume, then a membrane that stops the solute lets the water move, and a wilted lettuce leaf is the puzzle we return to at the end.
Each screen adds one condition: concentration is amount per volume, water goes towards the solute, volumes change while the solute stays, and a cell wall pushes back.
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): bio-water-across-a-membrane-2, -4, -conc-check. Their meaning is covered in the teaching screens.

lesson.title: When only water can cross

lead.text: Start with a cup of squash. Two spoonfuls of syrup stirred into a litre of water make a drink of a certain strength. Stir the same two spoonfuls into two litres instead and the drink tastes weaker, even though it holds exactly as much syrup. What changed is how much water the syrup is spread through.

In the last lesson the two compartments were the same size, so comparing amounts was enough. When the volumes differ, the strength of a solution is its concentration: the amount of solute divided by the volume it is dissolved in. The first drink has 2 spoonfuls in 1 litre, which is 2 spoonfuls per litre. The second has 2 spoonfuls in 2 litres, which is 1 spoonful per litre.

This gives a rule we will use all through the lesson. Adding water adds volume and no solute, so the concentration falls. Taking water away does the reverse and makes the solution stronger. The solute that was there stays there whatever happens to the water, and only the volume it fills changes.
One side of a membrane holds some solute in a known volume.
Now a jug in place of the cup.

Now put a membrane into the cup. Picture a container split in two by a membrane that lets water through and stops the solute. A membrane that passes some substances and blocks others like this is selectively permeable. Water crosses it in both directions, as it would cross any open gap.

Take two sides of equal size, one holding little solute and the other a lot. Solute particles take up room, so the side with more solute holds less water in each litre. By the rule from the last lesson, a substance drifts from where it is more crowded to where it is less crowded. For the water that means towards the side with more solute. The solute can't follow, because the membrane stops it, so the water goes to where the solute is. This net movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane towards the side with more solute is called osmosis.

afterFigure.text: Move the slider and watch the dashed line between the two sides. The solute stays where it is, and the line slides as water crosses, until the two sides are equally concentrated. The side that gained water ends up larger. In these pictures nothing pushes on either side, so only the solute decides which way the water goes.

lead.text: The solute can't leave its own side, so only the water moves.
As the dashed line slides, the volumes change while the solute stays put, so the concentrations change too. To predict by how much, follow one side at a time.

Take a side with 6 units of solute in volume 2. Its concentration is 6 ÷ 2 = 3 units per volume. Now water enters until the volume is 3. The solute has not crossed, so it is still 6 units and the new concentration is 6 ÷ 3 = 2. More volume with the same solute makes a weaker solution.

Water leaving works in reverse. Take 12 units in volume 3, a concentration of 4. Water leaving takes none of the solute with it, so if water leaves until the volume is 2, the same 12 units are crowded into less space and the concentration becomes 12 ÷ 2 = 6. Volume and concentration move in opposite directions: doubling the volume halves the concentration, and halving the volume doubles it.
A real membrane has two sides, and both change at once. The side that gains water grows weaker and the side that loses it grows stronger, until the two concentrations match.
Keep the solute fixed and change the volume.
Back to the lettuce. The cells of the leaf have solute dissolved inside them, and the plain water in the bowl has none. By what we have just worked out, water moves into the cells.

In our pictures nothing pushes back, so water would keep entering for as long as the inside held more solute than the outside. A leaf cell is different. It sits inside the stiff cell wall we met in the first lesson, so when water enters the cell swells and presses against the wall. The wall presses back. The more water gets in, the harder the wall pushes.
The salty bowl has the opposite effect. The outside now holds more solute than the inside, so water leaves, the cells shrink away from their walls and lose their firmness, and the leaf goes limp.
Pressure is a second influence on how water moves, alongside the solute. Our diagrams leave it out, so a prediction about a real plant cell has to allow for it.
A plant cell sits in plain water, and water starts to enter it.

lesson.orientation: Predict osmosis without confusing solute amount with concentration.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Put a wilted lettuce leaf in a bowl of plain water for half an hour and it turns crisp again. Put a fresh leaf in a bowl of very salty water and it goes limp. Nobody has cut or heated either leaf, and the cells in both are wrapped in the same kind of membrane.

The last lesson ended with a membrane that passes water and stops a solute. A leaf cell's membrane behaves in just that way: most of what is dissolved in the cell and in the bowl is held back, while water can cross. That leaves water as the only thing free to move, so the answer must lie in where the water goes.
This lesson follows the water. To say where it goes, we first need a way of saying how strong a solution is, so we start with a cup of squash.

intro.promise: By the end you'll predict which way water moves across a membrane when solute cannot, and work out how concentrations change.

recap.keyIdea: When only water can cross a membrane, it moves towards the side with more solute. The solute stays put, so volumes and concentrations change.

blocks.text: You diluted a drink, followed water towards the more concentrated side, and worked out new concentrations as the volume changed. That is enough to explain the lettuce. In plain water its cells take in water until the walls push back and the leaf turns crisp, and in salty water they lose water and the leaf goes limp.

recap.nextHook: Cells also run chemical reactions that would be far too slow on their own, and the next lesson compares two beakers to see what a helper molecule does.

questions.prompt: Water can cross but solute cannot. Equal volumes hold 4 solute units on the left and 12 on the right, at equal pressure. Which side gains water at first?
hints: Compare the amounts of solute. The volumes are equal.
Which side holds less water in each litre?
Water drifts from where it is more crowded to where it is less crowded.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The right side is more concentrated in solute, so it initially gains water.

questions.onCorrect: The right side, where the solute is more concentrated. Water moves towards more solute.

misconceptions.feedback: The left side has less solute. Water moves towards the more concentrated side, not away from it.

questions.prompt: As water enters the right compartment, what happens to its 12 solute units?
hints: The membrane's selectivity stays the same.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The membrane blocks solute; only its concentration changes.

questions.onCorrect: They stay. Only the water moves, so the solute is simply spread through a bigger volume.

misconceptions.feedback: Solute is never destroyed. It stays where it is.
The membrane blocks the solute, so it cannot cross.

questions.prompt: A compartment contains 12 solute units in volume 2. What is its concentration in units per volume?
hints: Use amount divided by volume.
Identify the amount and the volume in the question.
Divide the amount by the volume.
questions.onCorrect: 6 per volume. Concentration is the amount of solute divided by the volume.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the amount by the volume. Concentration divides.
That's the amount alone. Divide by the volume.

questions.prompt: Why can the two volumes change while the total solute stays constant?
hints: Follow each substance separately.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Changing the water distribution changes volumes without changing solute amount.

questions.onCorrect: Water moves and solute stays, so volumes change but each side's solute amount does not.

misconceptions.feedback: Solute stays solute. Only the water moves across.
Nothing creates solute here. Its amount is fixed on each side.

questions.prompt: A compartment contains 8 units of trapped solute. Its volume increases from 1 to 2. By what factor is its concentration multiplied?
hints: Calculate the concentration before and after.
The solute amount is unchanged.
Divide the new concentration by the old one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Concentration changes from 8 to 4, a factor of 4 ÷ 8 = 0.5.

questions.onCorrect: 0.5. Doubling the volume halves the concentration when the solute amount is fixed.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be a doubling. The volume grew, so the concentration fell.
That's the new concentration, not the factor between old and new.

questions.prompt: A plant cell wall builds an opposing pressure as water enters. Which prediction is justified?
hints: The real cell includes a force that the model leaves out.

acceptedIdeas: Pressure can reduce or stop net water entry
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Water movement depends on both solute concentration and pressure; the simple partition model omits this opposition.

choices.label: Water must keep entering without limit
Pressure can reduce or stop net water entry

questions.onCorrect: Pressure can reduce or stop net entry. Water movement depends on pressure as well as solute.

misconceptions.feedback: That ignores the wall. As the cell swells, the wall pushes back.
Nothing in the wall's pushing damages the membrane. The pressure just opposes more water entering.

questions.prompt: Water can cross but solute cannot. Equal volumes at equal pressure hold 9 solute units on the left and 3 on the right. Which side gains water at first?
hints: Which side is more concentrated?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The left side has more solute, so it gains water.

questions.onCorrect: The left side. It is the more concentrated, so water moves towards it.

misconceptions.feedback: The right side has less solute. Water moves towards more solute.

questions.prompt: A compartment of volume 4 holds 20 units of trapped solute. Water leaves until its volume is 2. What is its concentration now?
hints: Water leaving does not take solute with it.
Keep the amount of solute unchanged.
Divide the amount by the new volume.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The solute stays at 20: 20 ÷ 2 = 10 units per volume.

questions.onCorrect: 10 per volume. Losing water with the same solute makes the solution more concentrated.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the concentration before water left. The volume is smaller now, so the solute is more crowded.

questions.prompt: A jug holds 6 spoonfuls of syrup in 2 litres of drink. You top it up with water, adding no more syrup, until it holds 4 litres. How many spoonfuls of syrup are there per litre now?
hints: Water adds volume, not syrup.
How much syrup is there, and how many litres?
Divide the syrup by the litres.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The syrup is still 6 spoonfuls. 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 spoonfuls per litre.

questions.onCorrect: 1.5. Adding water spreads the same syrup through more volume, so the drink is weaker.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the strength before topping up. More water makes the drink weaker.
That's the total spoonfuls. The question asks how many per litre.

questions.prompt: You add water to a solution without adding any solute. Does it become more or less concentrated?
hints: The same solute is now spread through more volume.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The same solute in more volume gives a lower concentration.

questions.onCorrect: Less concentrated. The same solute is spread through more volume.

misconceptions.feedback: Adding water adds volume but no solute, so the solute is more spread out.

questions.prompt: A compartment holds 20 solute units in volume 5. Water enters until its volume is 10. What is its concentration now?
hints: The solute cannot cross, so how much is there still?
Use the new volume, not the old one.
Divide the amount by the new volume.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The solute amount is unchanged: 20 ÷ 10 = 2 units per volume.

questions.onCorrect: 2 per volume. The amount stayed fixed while the volume doubled, so the concentration halved.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the concentration before water entered. Use the new volume.
That's the amount of solute alone. Divide it by the volume to get the concentration.
